high_priority_articles.summary: Major CBAM Shake-Up: EU Reportedly Plans To Exempt UK Imports From January 2026  Carbon Herald
high_priority_articles.full_text:
- A leaked draft EU-UK summit declaration reportedly proposes exempting British goods from the EU CBAM, retroactively from January 1, 2026.
- The proposal is linked to an agreement to connect the EU ETS and UK ETS, potentially removing carbon-related trade costs between the two markets.
- The exemption remains unconfirmed and would require the necessary legal steps before companies could rely on it.
The European Union could be preparing a significant change to its Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (EU CBAM), with British goods potentially receiving an exemption dating back to January 1, 2026.
A draft declaration reportedly points to progress on linking the UK ETS and EU ETS, a development that could reshape carbon-related trade between the two economies. However, the proposed CBAM exemption has not yet become law.
The development was first reported by Rapporteur, which obtained access to a draft declaration prepared ahead of the November 20 EU-UK summit in Brussels. The document reportedly indicates that linking the two carbon markets could allow British goods to avoid the EU’s carbon levy, including retrospectively from the beginning of 2026.
ETS Linkage Could Change Cross-Channel Trade
The proposed arrangement builds on commitments made during the May 2025 EU-UK summit. In its Common Understanding, both parties agreed to pursue a formal link between their respective emissions trading systems, with the intention of enabling mutual exemptions from their CBAM regimes.
The European Council subsequently authorised negotiations on ETS linkage in November 2025, explicitly identifying reciprocal CBAM exemptions as a potential benefit. The UK government has also confirmed that negotiations are underway.
For businesses, the implications could be substantial. EU importers purchasing British steel, aluminium, cement, fertilisers and other covered products could potentially avoid CBAM obligations on qualifying UK-origin goods. British manufacturers would also benefit from reduced administrative requirements and potentially improved access to European customers.
Legal Questions Remain Over Retroactive Exemption
Despite the reported progress, the proposal would require changes to EU legislation, subject to approval by both the European Parliament and the Council.
Article 2(6) of the EU CBAM Regulation requires a fully linked emissions trading system agreement and an effective carbon price for a third country to qualify for exemption. The relevant country must also be included in Annex III.
The proposed January 2026 starting date raises further questions because the EU’s definitive CBAM regime only began operating on that date. The legal mechanism for applying an exemption retrospectively has not been publicly established.
Reciprocal Benefits And The Road Ahead
The UK is preparing its own CBAM for January 2027. Its Finance Act 2026 provides powers to exclude goods originating in jurisdictions with linked emissions trading systems, creating a potential route to reciprocal treatment for EU exporters.
The November 20 summit could provide further political clarity, although Reuters and the Financial Times have reported that some elements of the broader EU-UK package may require additional negotiations after the meeting.
Until the linking agreement is concluded and the necessary legislation takes effect, companies should continue following existing reporting and compliance requirements. Nevertheless, the reported proposal signals a potentially important acceleration in EU-UK carbon-market integration, with consequences extending well beyond the CBAM itself.

high_priority_articles.full_text:
THE election results in America this week portend a sea change, and they have important ramifications for Pakistan. The Democrats have taken both the House and the Senate in a rout that reached Texas and Kansas. Anger over living costs, tariffs, and the war on Iran all played their part. For the remaining two years of his term, President Donald Trump will face a Congress armed with subpoena power and eager to use it.
This is no distant affair for us. Much of the world has spent two years trying to cope with Trump. Meanwhile, the leadership in Pakistan flamboyantly embraced him, though let’s not underestimate how well that worked. It got us lower tariffs, a White House lunch, and, above all, a central role when the Iran war needed an exit ramp. The question now is what that embrace will cost us as the man on the receiving end of it begins to lose his grip on Washington.
Pakistan has veered too close to Trump, and this might not go down well in the near future. The April ceasefire that we helped broker was a genuine achievement, and I said so at the time. The memorandum that followed in June has since collapsed, but the credit earned in those weeks still stands. Yet all of it could well come to be overshadowed by the single act of having nominated Trump for a Nobel Peace Prize in so conspicuous and overly generous a manner.
Showering the man with extravagant praise in highly public settings might have worked to win him over in the short term. But the praise kept coming long after the point had been made. In September, he was telling the UN General Assembly that our prime minister credits him with saving 30 million lives. Last month, on the day the Nobel went to someone else, the prime minister was on X lauding his “historic role” in South Asia. These things do not expire. There is a risk they get tagged onto Pakistan in the years to come, once Americans settle on their verdict of this presidency.

What looks clever in one season reads very differently at a hearing in the next.

Even more dangerous is the fact that the Trump family’s business dealings might come under congressional investigation. Reuters reported in September that probes could begin as early as February, with Trump-linked crypto firms of particular interest. Senator Richard Blumenthal, who is in line to chair an investigations panel, has promised to use his subpoena power. The same senator was asking questions about World Liberty Financial’s Pakistan deal in May last year.
If any ties lead back here, they could tie the country to the affair; the threads are already in public view. In January, our finance minister signed a memorandum with a World Liberty affiliate concerning its USD1 stablecoin. In September, the defence ministry placed a limited order with Powerus, a drone company in which two of Trump’s sons are investors. No wrongdoing has been established. The White House denies any conflict of interest, and as of July the stablecoin deal had produced no known transactions at all. But I have described that memorandum as an instrument of access, and access is exactly what investigators will want to look into. What looks clever in one season reads very differently at a hearing in the next.
These risks, however, are rooted more in optics and perceptions than in realpolitik. Pakistan’s thrust to find a place in the new regional order emerging in the Middle East must continue unabated. The Makkah Joint Defence Agreement with Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, and the Tehran huddle I wrote about last week, which Field Marshal Asim Munir himself proposed, have a logic of their own that does not depend on who chairs which committee in Washington. Whatever the fallout for Pakistan, the changing of the political tide in America will be an American affair first and foremost.
The most likely outcome is that the Trump administration comes to be consumed by its wrangling with the new Congress and loses its moorings in foreign policy. A White House fighting hearings and subpoenas at home will have little bandwidth for the world.
This could produce a hazardous moment. A beleaguered and irrational president might try an adventure abroad to distract from his troubles at home, and the adventure is ready to hand. The blockade of Iran remains in place, reports in September said he saw a fresh bombing campaign as likely after the midterms, and Iran’s Supreme Leader warned on Wednesday that the war’s scope will widen if the attacks are repeated. But that seems unlikely given the stakes. This is the war voters have just punished him for, and on the eve of the vote he himself cast doubt on resuming strikes.
What is more likely is an acceleration in the pace with which America withdraws from its commitments to underwrite global order, particularly its military posture in the Middle East. I argued in April that the price of getting out of this war would be a disorderly exit from the region altogether. A Congress that owes its majority partly to anger over this war will be in no hurry to fund the next one. The Gulf monarchies have seen their American protector fail to shield them from Iranian missiles, and they are drawing their own conclusions. All this will spur the search for a new security architecture among the powers of the region, a search that will definitely include Pakistan.
Three times in our history, in the 1960s, the 1980s and the 2000s, an American embrace brought dollars and a growth spurt, and each time the money stopped when Washington’s interest moved on. This time it has brought more photographs than dollars. Ironically enough, this turning inward of the United States might just be the push Pakistan needs to learn to stand on its own feet.
The writer is a business and economy journalist.

The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) preliminarily finds that countervailable subsidies were provided to producers and exporters of ripe olives from Spain. Accordingly, the deadline for the preliminary results is now November 2, 2026.

Pursuant to 19 CFR 351.213(d)(3), it is Commerce's practice to rescind an administrative review of a countervailing duty order where it concludes that there were no suspended entries of subject merchandise during the POR.[9]
Normally, upon completion of an administrative review, the suspended entries are liquidated at the countervailing duty assessment rate calculated for the POR.[10]
Therefore, for an administrative review of a company to be conducted, there must be a reviewable, suspended entry that Commerce can instruct U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to liquidate at the countervailing duty assessment rate for the POR.[11]

high_priority_articles.title: How the UK-India Free Trade Agreement reshapes advanced manufacturing - ET Manufacturing
high_priority_articles.summary: How the UK-India Free Trade Agreement reshapes advanced manufacturing  ET Manufacturing
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The landmark UK-India Free Trade Agreement (FTA), formally known as the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) is creating opportunities in one of the world's fastest-growing industrial markets for British manufacturers. Here is what that means in practice for businesses.
The agreement came into force on 15 July this year, under its terms, 99% of Indian origin goods entering the UK and 90% of UK origin goods entering India will either be duty free or subject to reduced tariffs. It will benefit a wide range of industries on both sides including automotive, manufacturing, consumer goods, creative industries, and medical technology. The agreement marks the biggest milestone in the bilateral economic partnership to date. In the long run, the deal is expected to boost bilateral trade by £25.5 billion, Indian GDP by £5.1billion, and UK GDP by £4.8 billion every year.
When the UK and India signed the FTA in July 2025, it marked the biggest bilateral trade deal the UK has agreed since leaving the European Union and one of India’s most comprehensive trade deals ever.
For the UK, the calculation is different: it is about securing new anchors of growth for industry. Advanced manufacturing is one such anchor, a fact underpinned by the UK’s Modern Industrial Strategy, which places the sector at the top of its growth priorities. The FTA is, in effect, one of the most direct policy levers available to UK manufacturers looking to compete in Asia’s largest emerging market.
Why advanced manufacturing is central to the deal
Advanced manufacturing spans a cluster of sectors united by a reliance on automation, precision engineering, digital design tools, automotive electrification, scientific instruments and machinery, and advanced materials. These are precisely the sectors where UK firms lead, and where the FTA unlocks the greatest opportunity.
British aerospace, led by companies such as Rolls-Royce, BAE Systems, and supported by a deep network of specialist suppliers, is among the most sophisticated in the world. The UK is a significant exporter of turbojet engines, aircraft components, precision instruments, and the kind of high-specification machinery that underpins industrial production across multiple sectors.
How does the UK-Indi free trade agreement work?
A Free Trade Agreement or FTA is a formal treaty between two or more countries in which the parties primarily agree to reduce or eliminate barriers to the movement of goods and services between them. In practice, an FTA means that a product manufactured in Country A can enter Country B at a lower (or sometimes zero) import duty than it would otherwise face.
The UK and India are two major economies with deep commercial, cultural and people-to-people links. This agreement gives businesses greater confidence to trade, invest and collaborate across a fast-growing economic corridor. As a Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, it also addresses services, customs, intellectual property, government procurement, non-tariff barriers and other areas of cooperation.
Addressing non-tariff barriers
Tariffs are visible and quantifiable: a 100% duty on an imported car is a blunt and measurable obstacle. Non-tariff barriers (NTBs) are the subtler, often more stubborn impediments to trade: divergent product standards, cumbersome customs documentation requirements, opaque licensing regimes, and differing certification processes. A British machinery exporter might face zero tariff at India’s border, yet struggle to secure Indian certification for its equipment. The UK-India FTA addresses such friction points, committing both sides to simplifying documentation, accelerating customs clearance, and enabling UK conformity assessment bodies to certify certain products against Indian regulatory standards before goods even leave British shores.
Changes in tariff architecture
The tariff provisions of the UK-India FTA are structured around tariff-rate quotas (TRQs) for vehicles and immediate/staged tariff liberalisation schedule for other tariff lines.
This granular, product-by-product approach determines exactly what duties apply to which goods and when.
Aerospace: Among the most immediately impactful provisions for the UK’s advanced manufacturing is the treatment of aerospace components.
Tariffs on aircraft parts, which were as high as 11%, fell to zero from the first day the FTA entered into force.
For a sector defined by long supply chains and razor-thin margins on complex components, this is a structural shift in competitiveness.
Similarly, most scientific and technical measuring instruments, a category that encompasses the precision tools essential to both aerospace production and industrial quality control, get lower duty under the FTA.
Auto and Future Mobility: For this sector, the deal’s architecture is more phased, reflecting the political and economic sensitivity.
India’s automobile market is one of the most protected in the world, with import duties on fully assembled cars exceeding 100% in some cases, effectively pricing most foreign vehicles very highly.
The FTA changes this, but carefully.
The UK’s internal combustion engine vehicles gain access via a TRQ, with duties falling from their triple-digit starting point to a range of 30 to 50% initially, and eventually to 10% by year five.
The TRQ begins at 20,000 units in year 1 and rises to 37,000 by year 5.
Manufacturing, Textile Machinery and Industrial Technologies: For the UK’s wider manufacturing offer, the agreement is relevant where it lowers the cost base of the equipment underpinning India’s industrial modernization across machinery, electrical systems and automation.
Industrial machinery tariffs across many categories reduce to zero within five years.
Immediate tariff cuts on Robotics and automation (e.
g.
industrial robots to get tariff free entry into India) improve investment payback economics.
Tariffs on all Textile Machinery will be eliminated within 5 years.
Tariffs on most Test and Measurement equipment  will be reduced and become zero duty within ten years.
Deep reductions across electrical machinery strengthens the UK’s positions across advanced manufacturing supply chains.

Customs, Digital Trade and SMEs
Even the most ambitious tariff reductions mean little if goods are stuck at the border. A consignment of precision aircraft components that sits in a customs queue for three weeks is a problem for an aerospace manufacturer regardless of the duty rate. This is why the FTA’s provisions on customs and trade facilitation provisions matter as much as the tariff schedule itself.
Opening the procurement door
One of the most significant elements of the FTA is its chapter on government procurement. The deal includes India’s first comprehensive government procurement chapter in an FTA. Government procurement, in simple terms, covers how public bodies, including ministries, agencies, and state-owned enterprises, purchase goods and services. It is a large and steady source of demand in any economy, and one that governments have typically kept outside the scope of trade liberalisation.
The IP foundation
Advanced manufacturing is underpinned by innovation. Turbojet engines, precision machinery, and next-generation battery chemistry are the result of years of research and development (R&D), built on proprietary processes and deep engineering expertise. This know-how, often embedded in design, production techniques, and materials science, is what gives firms their competitive advantage.
When leadership signals commitment
Political will drive the momentum of -behind any trade agreement, and the UK-India FTA has had no shortage of it.
Vision 2035
The UK and India have also endorsed ‘Vision 2035’ - an ambitious, future-focused agreement which underscores the two nations’ resolve to work together for mutual growth, prosperity and to help shape a secure, and sustainable world at a time of rapid global change. This Vision 2035 embeds the trade deal within a more ambitious agenda: structured collaboration on frontier technologies that will define the next generation of advanced manufacturing.

Facts
European Commission confirms Ukraine meets conditions to open all EU accession negotiating clusters – PM
The European Commission has confirmed that Ukraine has met the conditions for opening all remaining negotiating clusters in its EU accession process, while its progress in preparing for membership has improved in nine chapters, Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky said.
"Today, the European Commission's report was personally handed to me by EU Ambassador to Ukraine Katarina Mathernova. The European Commission confirmed that Ukraine has met the conditions for opening all remaining clusters. The state of preparation for accession has improved in nine chapters. This is more than twice as many as last year. There has been no deterioration in any chapter, nor any rollback of reforms," Koretsky wrote on Telegram on Wednesday.
He said the European Commission had noted good or very good progress in 10 chapters, including energy, the digital sector, financial services, taxation, education, science, agriculture and customs.
He also said that, for the first time, foreign policy, security and defense had received the highest progress assessment. The European Commission also noted the independent and effective work of Ukraine's anti-corruption institutions, as well as improved assessments in the areas of the judiciary and justice.
"The next goal is to receive an Interim Benchmark Assessment Report (IBAR) in early 2027. To this end, at the initiative of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, a joint Ukraine-EU working group has been established. We are setting ambitious but achievable goals. There are areas where we need to work faster. We are taking the European Commission's recommendations forward," Koretsky said.

ISLAMABAD: Despite having Generalised Scheme of Preferences (GSP+) status, Pakistan’s exports to major western and eastern European markets fell in the first quarter of 2026-27 compared with the previous year.

Overall exports to Europe dipped modestly, with a slight increase in proceeds from southern and northern European countries during the July-September quarter, raising serious concerns for policymakers.

The ongoing Middle East conflict has accelerated the decline in exports to these markets, along with the European Union’s preferential market access offered to India, one of Pakistan’s key competitors in textiles.

Data compiled by the State Bank of Pakistan showed that exports to European countries contracted 1.84pc to $2.350 billion in 1QFY27 from $2.394bn a year ago.

Trade analysts warn that the Middle East conflict could further dampen export demand, as rising energy costs are likely to squeeze consumer spending in Europe, which is already under strain from the economic fallout of the Ukraine war.

Exports to northern Europe increased by 21.07pc to $236.321m in 1QFY27 from $195.191m a year ago.

Exports to southern Europe grew 5.26pc to $879.896m in 1QFY27 from $835.862m in the corresponding period last year. In this region, exports to Spain rose 17.78pc to $451.244m from $383.122m in the preceding year.

Exports to Italy declined 8.49pc to $298.731m in 1QFY27, compared with $326.460m in the same period last year. Exports to Greece grew 3.52pc to $34.961m during the months under review, compared with $33.774m over the previous year.

However, exports to eastern Europe fell 15.05pc to $168.761m in 1QFY27 from $198.677m.

Before Brexit, the United Kingdom was Pakistan’s major export destination. In the post-Brexit period, Pakistan’s exports to the UK increased 6.64pc to $612.305m in 1QFY27 from $574.171m a year ago.

Western Europe, which includes countries such as Germany, the Netherlands, France, Italy, and Belgium, accounts for the largest share of Pakistan’s exports to the EU. However, exports to this region shrank 8.51pc to $1.065bn in 1QFY27 from $1.164bn in 1QFY26.

Exports to Germany dipped 12.77pc to $389.116m in 1QFY27 from $446.100m. Similarly, exports to the Netherlands, the second-largest market for Pakistani goods, fell by 3.07pc to $370.005m from $381.752m a year ago.

Exports to France fell by 0.47pc to $136.030m in 1QFY27 from $136.686m, followed by a 7.57pc decline to Belgium’s $127.431m against $137.871m.

high_priority_articles.summary: COP31: EU FTA on horizon, but India won't budge on CBAM  The Economic Times
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The minister said barriers linked to cost, intellectual property and trade must be done away with as these prevent smaller countries from getting the benefit of better technologies. India and the EU are expected to sign the FTA by mid-December. The agreement would allow duty-free access to several of India's labour-intensive sectors such as leather, textiles, gems and jewellery, besides tariff concessions to a large segment of EU imports.
The highly contested CBAM regime, which came into effect in January 2026, remains a prickly point as it impacts several Indian sectors from iron and steel to fertilisers, hydrogen and electricity, cement and aluminium among others. CBAM, in fact, will persist as a major point of contention at COP31, as developing nations, the G77 and the BASIC group have repeatedly been raising concerns over unilateral trade barriers besides climate finance and just transition concerns. India is part of all three blocs. The European Commission, on its part, is expected to host an event at COP31 on November 17, titled 'The State of the EU CBAM: What makes CBAM a success?'.
Another flashpoint between developing nations and the EU could emerge over its strong pitch for clean, or non-fossil, fuel-linked 'electrification' - a proposal mooted by COP31 presidency Turkiye to increase electricity's share in global energy consumption from 23% to 35% by 2035. Speaking to reporters, Yadav, however, sought to emphasise that voluntary initiatives under the Presidency Action Agenda should remain separate from negotiations and that "uniform global targets must respect national circumstances".
Turkiye is hosting the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in the city of Antalya from November 9 to 20. Australia acts as the president of negotiations. Yadav underlined that India would play a constructive, bridge-building role in Antalya, seeking an outcome that moves from commitments to implementation and support. Yadav, however, also reminded of the centrality of climate finance - an obligation of developed countries under Article 9.1 that must be "predictable, largely public and concessional, and should not add to the debt burden".
India's engagements at COP31 will include LeadIT 3.0 with Sweden, in addition to high-level side events on coastal resilience, panels on the International Big Cat Alliance and forests.

high_priority_articles.summary: Draft import-export strategy: How can Vietnamese businesses avoid remaining perpetually behind FDI?  Vietnam.vn
high_priority_articles.full_text:
(NB&CL) The draft Strategy for Import and Export of Goods until 2030, with a vision to 2045, aims for an average annual export growth of 15-16%, while increasing the proportion of domestic enterprises to 28-30% by 2030.
In recent years, import and export trade has consistently maintained double-digit growth, forming a crucial driving force for Vietnam's economy . In 2024, total import and export turnover reached US$786.29 billion, an increase of 15.4% compared to the previous year. In 2025, this figure is projected to exceed US$930 billion, an increase of over 18%.
According to the latest report from the General Statistics Office of the Ministry of Finance , in the first 10 months of 2026, Vietnam's total import and export turnover reached US$1,010.55 billion, an increase of 32.3% compared to the same period last year.
The General Statistics Office emphasized that this is the first time Vietnam's merchandise trade has exceeded the $1 trillion mark, setting an all-time high. This result reflects the ever-expanding scale of international trade and demonstrates the growing role of import and export in the economy.
Speaking with a reporter from the Newspaper of Journalists and Public Opinion, Dr. Huynh Thanh Dien, an economic expert, said that the fact that import and export turnover will exceed the 1,000 billion USD mark in 2026 has been predicted beforehand.
According to him, the impressive growth in import and export activities in recent times has been largely contributed by the foreign direct investment (FDI) sector.
Data for the first 10 months of 2026 shows that, on the export side, total turnover reached nearly 500 billion USD. Of this, FDI accounted for 81.2% of the total turnover, while domestic enterprises accounted for only 18.8%.
This disparity is also reflected in imports. Of the total import value of $511.31 billion, the FDI sector accounted for 74.2%, while domestic enterprises accounted for approximately 25.8%.
Dr. Huynh Thanh Dien explained that, thanks to a stable investment environment, skillful policies, and an increasingly expanding network of free trade agreements (FTAs), Vietnam is becoming an attractive destination for international investment capital.
Furthermore, strategic competition between the US and China is leading some businesses to expand or relocate their production facilities to neighboring countries in order to optimize costs.
“ Vietnam is one of the preferred destinations thanks to its advantageous geographical location, investment environment, and connectivity with international markets ,” said Dr. Huynh Thanh Dien.
Therefore, many FDI enterprises choose Vietnam as a production base for export goods, thereby creating an important impetus for Vietnam's international trade growth.
An ambitious goal
You may also like
Building on its achievements, the Ministry of Industry and Trade is developing a draft strategy for goods import and export until 2030, with a vision to 2045. The draft aims for an average annual growth rate of 15-16% in goods export turnover and 12-13% in imports during the 2026-2030 period.
According to many experts, this is considered an ambitious goal, but it is not without a basis for achievement.
According to Mr. Nguyen Tuan Viet, General Director of VIETGO and an expert in the import-export field, total import-export turnover is a very important indicator reflecting the strength of the economy.
" To become a superpower and build a strong nation, Vietnam first needs strong growth in total import and export turnover ," he said.
According to Mr. Viet, Vietnam already has many favorable foundations to achieve the target of an average annual growth rate of 15-16% in merchandise exports.
First and foremost are the strategic steps taken by the Government over the past 20 years, particularly the expansion of the network of free trade agreements (FTAs) and the implementation of an effective foreign policy.
Furthermore, Resolution 68, issued in 2025, marked a significant milestone by affirming the role and position of entrepreneurs and businesses in the economy, while identifying the private sector as one of the most important driving forces of the national economy.
" Accordingly, ministries, sectors, and agencies need to focus on supporting the development of businesses. I believe this is a strategically significant step by the Government ," he said.
The next driving force comes from the agility and adaptability of the business community. Vietnamese businesses have been actively learning from the experience of FDI enterprises, while also improving in both production and sales.
In particular, over the last three to four years, we have gradually formed the sales force of the economy, which are trading companies.
"These are businesses that don't directly own manufacturing facilities but purchase goods from domestic production facilities for export. The development of this group is very positive, helping Vietnam become more proactive in sales and access to international markets," Mr. Viet shared.
Creating room for domestic businesses to thrive.
Besides the goal of maintaining growth momentum, the Draft Strategy for Goods Import and Export until 2030, with a vision to 2045, also aims to enhance the role of domestic enterprises and increase the processing and technological content in exported goods.
The draft aims for the proportion of export turnover from domestic enterprises in the total national export turnover to reach approximately 28% - 30% by 2030, increasing to 38% - 40% by 2045.
Dr. Huynh Thanh Dien assessed that Vietnam needs to directly address the issue of FDI enterprises' export value significantly surpassing that of domestic businesses, and then find a "solution" to this goal.
You may also like
He analyzed that currently, the FDI business sector has a trade surplus, meaning the value of exports is greater than imports. Meanwhile, the domestic business sector has a trade deficit, importing not only machinery, equipment, and components but also consumer goods, including items that the country is capable of producing domestically.
"If a portion of imported goods are replaced by products made by domestic businesses, we will create more opportunities for investment, technological innovation, and jobs. Workers will have better incomes, purchasing power will increase, and this will contribute back to growth," he said.
Therefore, Dr. Huynh Thanh Dien believes that Vietnam has been successful in attracting foreign investment, but the next step is to build a sufficiently strong domestic production base. Only when domestic businesses develop will the economy have a foundation for sustainable long-term growth.
Regarding solutions, this expert suggested that Vietnam should use public investment as a tool to activate domestic production capacity.
Currently, Vietnam is implementing numerous infrastructure projects in transportation, energy, and information technology. When developing these projects, it is necessary to clearly identify which domestic enterprises can participate, which enterprises can play a leading role, and which small and medium-sized enterprises can supply products and services.
For products that Vietnamese businesses can produce, opportunities should be created for them to participate. For example, suitable bidding packages could be designed, joint ventures with domestic businesses could be encouraged, and a certain percentage of public procurement could be allocated to small and medium-sized enterprises, based on compliance with relevant regulations.
“ Many products that we currently import to serve public works projects, in my opinion, domestic businesses could absolutely produce. The problem is that the opportunities haven't been clearly presented. If we keep importing inputs to expedite project implementation, domestic businesses will lose opportunities to invest, master technology, and grow, ” he said.

SA exporters face Agoa setback, but broader US trade ties remain intact
While the loss of preferential access could put thousands of jobs at risk, the economic consequences are manageable if government and business work together to identify alternative markets and trade opportunities, says NWU Business School economist, Raymond Parsons.
He argues that the development should serve as a catalyst for accelerating export diversification, strengthening regional and international trade partnerships and improving South Africa’s global competitiveness.
"Although the loss of Agoa preferences is highly regrettable and the specific sectoral impact may be painful, the situation is manageable if the right market adaptations are made," Parsons says. "Addressing the negative economic consequences of losing Agoa preferences will therefore continue to require close collaboration between government and the relevant business interests to identify alternative trade strategies."
Despite the Agoa decision, non-Agoa trade relations with the US remain far more substantial, with the overwhelming bulk of SA’s exports to that country falling outside Agoa preferences, Parsons says.
"This trade then drives the vast majority of existing bilateral economic ties between SA and the US. The non-Agoa trade relationships are therefore reinforced by a robust footprint that goes beyond trade balances. The Agoa result still means that the core economic pipeline of trade and investment connecting SA and the US remains intact, and must continue to be nurtured."
Adapting to trade shifts
Nevertheless, Parsons says the exclusion reinforces two priorities for South Africa.
"First, SA must accelerate its market diversification strategy in a changing geoeconomic world that offers new opportunities. Enlarging and diversifying trade options includes expanding East Asian market access to growing economies there, as well as further leveraging economic opportunities through the African Continental Free Trade Agreement (AfCFTA)," Parsons notes.
"Secondly, the government must aim to make the domestic economy more internationally competitive by reducing the costs of doing business in SA. This in particular encompasses expediting logistics reform, especially in rail and port facilities, that will help to offset the Agoa loss by keeping SA globally competitive.
"Ultimately, South Africa's ability to absorb the impact of losing Agoa preferences will depend less on the loss itself than on how quickly it adapts," Parsons adds.
He argues that diversifying export markets, strengthening trade partnerships and addressing domestic competitiveness constraints will be essential to keeping exporters globally competitive and sustaining the country's broader trade and investment relationships.

high_priority_articles.summary: South Korea's $350 Billion U.S. Investment Faces Uncertainty, With Tariff Policy Holding Firm  Businesskorea
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Shift in Congressional Control Leaves Executive Tariff Powers Intact, While State-Level Changes and Congressional Scrutiny Add to Investment Uncertainty
Following the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections, Democrats secured majorities in both chambers of Congress, shifting the balance of political power. However, analysts say tariff policies affecting South Korean companies are unlikely to change significantly, as the executive branch retains authority to impose tariffs under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act and Section 301 of the Trade Act, even as congressional oversight increases.
President Donald Trump is expected to continue pursuing his existing tariff and investment policies despite the shift in congressional control. Even if Democrats seek to amend legislation to limit the president's tariff authority, overriding a presidential veto would require a two-thirds majority in both the House and Senate, making significant legislative changes difficult to achieve.
South Korea's $350 billion investment commitment in the United States now faces uncertainty stemming from changes in state leadership and increased congressional scrutiny. In particular, the first major project, construction of the Encinal gas-fired combined-cycle power plant in Texas, could face delays following the election of Gina Hinojosa as governor. Hinojosa campaigned on pausing approvals for new data centers. With the first $2.4 billion installment already transferred, delays in local permitting could affect subsequent investment tranches.
The $350 billion investment commitment between South Korea and the United States comprises $200 billion in strategic-industry investment and $150 billion in shipbuilding cooperation. However, the only project currently confirmed is the Encinal power plant, while other initiatives, including nuclear power plant construction and Alaska liquefied natural gas (LNG) development, remain subject to further planning and implementation steps.
Nuclear power and grid investment retain potential for bipartisan cooperation, given the shared challenge of rising electricity demand driven by the expansion of artificial intelligence. The second major investment project under discussion involves building eight large nuclear reactors in the United States, with a total estimated value of $120 billion. A $10 billion advance payment is planned by year-end. However, changes to permitting reviews or construction schedules could increase financing and construction costs.
The semiconductor industry is closely watching whether the investment tax credit of up to 35%, scheduled to expire at year-end, will be extended. Texas is also set for changes in both federal and state leadership: Democrat James Talarico won the state's U.S. Senate race, while Gina Hinojosa was elected governor. The change in the governor's office could affect state-level tax and permitting priorities. Samsung Electronics is scheduled to begin construction of its second foundry plant in Taylor, Texas, in November, while SK hynix is considering New York as a potential site for a new NAND production facility by its subsidiary Solidigm. If the tax credit expires as scheduled on Dec. 31, 2026, facilities that begin construction after that date will be ineligible. Both parties have raised the possibility of extending the program, but the eligibility period and scope of support will depend on subsequent legislation.
Expanding semiconductor production in the United States and reducing supply-chain dependence on China remain shared policy goals of both parties, suggesting that pressure on South Korean companies to make additional U.S. investments will continue. At the same time, changes in regulations governing AI data center construction and policies related to electricity and water supply could affect major technology companies' infrastructure spending and, in turn, demand for memory chips.
High tariffs on automobiles and steel are also likely to remain in place. The 15% tariff on imported vehicles and tariffs of up to 50% on major steel products reflect the broader emphasis both parties place on protecting U.S. manufacturing, making a near-term easing of the measures difficult to anticipate. In response, South Korean companies such as Hyundai Motor Group and POSCO are moving ahead with plans to expand their U.S. production capacity.
The automotive and battery industries are also monitoring possible changes to state-level investment incentives and industrial policies following the gubernatorial transition in Georgia. Hyundai Motor Group's Metaplant America, Kia's manufacturing plant and SK On's battery facility are all located in the state. If the 15% tariff on imported vehicles and parts remains in place, Hyundai Motor and Kia will continue to face additional costs. Shinhan Investment & Securities estimates that the two companies' combined tariff costs could reach as much as 7.6 trillion won this year.
The possible reinstatement of electric-vehicle purchase subsidies, which the battery industry has been seeking, also remains uncertain. Even if Democrats pursue expanded support, the president could veto such legislation, leaving the prospects for a policy reversal unclear. Meanwhile, the Advanced Manufacturing Production Tax Credit under Section 45X, which supports battery production in the United States, is expected to remain in place. However, eligibility may be restricted based on ownership links to entities from countries of concern, including China, and the sourcing of raw materials. Managing dependence on Chinese materials will therefore remain important for South Korean battery makers.
The steel industry also expects high tariffs to persist. The United States currently imposes tariffs of 50% on major imported steel products and 25% on certain derivative products. POSCO and Hyundai Steel, together with Hyundai Motor and Kia, are investing a total of $5.8 billion in Louisiana to build an electric arc furnace steelworks with an annual production capacity of 2.7 million tons. The facility is targeted to begin operations in 2029. If tariffs remain in place, securing local production capacity in the United States will become increasingly important.
The $150 billion South Korea-U.S. shipbuilding cooperation initiative known as MASGA is likely to maintain its broad framework, but the possibility of building naval vessels overseas remains uncertain. Lawmakers from both parties have generally taken a cautious stance toward overseas construction of naval vessels. A compromise proposal included in the National Defense Authorization Act would allow allied companies that invest in U.S. shipyards to build up to two noncombat support vessels at overseas shipyards. The key question is how differences between Congress and the executive branch will be reconciled, following a presidential memorandum issued by the Trump administration in August 2026 that allowed certain vessels to be built by allied countries.
The Alaska LNG development project also faces uncertainty over its commercial viability and increased congressional oversight. The environmental and energy policy priorities advanced by Democrats could affect federal support and budget allocations for fossil-fuel development projects. At the same time, closer congressional scrutiny of project viability could lead to more thorough assessments of investment costs and profitability.
Grid expansion and renewable energy projects also face uncertainty amid potential policy changes. Both parties recognize the need to invest in transmission networks and power infrastructure to meet rising electricity demand from data centers. However, decisions on extending or restoring renewable-energy tax credits and related budget allocations will depend on congressional deliberations. These projects could create opportunities for South Korean power-equipment and energy-storage-system companies, although the scale and timing of potential contracts will depend on policy decisions and actual investment implementation.
Meanwhile, an ongoing Section 301 investigation by the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative into structural excess capacity in manufacturing, covering 16 economies including South Korea, represents another potential trade risk. Depending on the findings, the investigation could lead to additional tariffs, requiring South Korean companies to prepare for measures beyond the existing bilateral tariff arrangements. U.S. efforts to prevent Chinese goods from being rerouted through third countries could also increase compliance requirements for South Korean companies, particularly in documenting product origins and managing supply chains.
Jang Sang-sik, head of the Korea International Trade Association's Institute for International Trade, said South Korea should retain the ability to adjust or suspend further investment outflows if projects encounter difficulties. He also stressed the need to monitor developments in the United States and ensure that safeguards established in advance — including payment and repayment terms and profit-sharing arrangements — function as intended.

Major US businesses are divided over whether the Trump administration should impose additional tariffs on Vietnamese goods, with Tesla and Samsung warning that higher duties could disrupt supply chains, while American producers and intellectual property groups are urging Washington to take a tougher approach.
The disagreement emerged in submissions to the US government ahead of a November 29 deadline for concluding a trade investigation into Vietnam’s alleged intellectual property violations. The probe, launched in May, follows Washington’s decision to designate Vietnam a “priority foreign country”, placing it in the most serious category of the US intellectual property watchlist for the first time in 13 years.
The United States has accused Vietnam of a “persistent failure to resolve long-standing concerns about IP protection and enforcement”. A separate investigation into alleged excess industrial capacity is also underway, adding another source of trade uncertainty for the Southeast Asian economy.

Vietnam has urged Washington to conduct its investigations objectively. It remains unclear whether any tariffs arising from the intellectual property investigation would apply broadly across Vietnamese imports or target specific industries.
The United States currently imposes a general 12.5% tariff on Vietnamese goods, introduced in July following an investigation into alleged failures to prevent imports of products made with forced labor. Vietnam had previously faced a 20% tariff under President Donald Trump’s “Liberation Day” trade measures, but the Supreme Court struck down those duties.
Many economists have argued that the administration’s objective is to restore tariffs at least at the level previously imposed before the court ruling. A new trade action linked to intellectual property enforcement could provide another route to higher duties, although the scope and legal basis of any additional measures remain unresolved.
Tesla urged the US Trade Representative to consider the supply chain requirements of American manufacturers before imposing further tariffs. In comments submitted on July 2, the electric vehicle maker said some advanced components and precision manufacturing equipment could not be sourced domestically, even after substantial investment in US production.
The company’s position highlights a constraint facing manufacturers seeking to expand domestic production: US factories remain dependent on international suppliers for certain specialized inputs. Tariffs on Vietnamese goods could therefore raise costs for American companies if affected products or components are difficult to replace with domestic alternatives.
Samsung’s US unit made a similar submission, pointing to Vietnam’s importance in manufacturing smartphones and network equipment supplied to the American market. The South Korean technology group is Vietnam’s largest foreign investor, with approximately $25 billion invested in the country.
Retail organizations and trade associations representing businesses with extensive manufacturing operations in Vietnam also opposed additional tariffs. Their members include footwear and apparel companies, as well as manufacturers of consumer products such as bicycles and video game consoles.
For these businesses, the issue extends beyond the direct cost of imported finished goods. Higher tariffs could affect established production networks, supplier relationships, and the economics of products assembled in Vietnam for US consumers.
Vietnam’s expanding trade position adds to the significance of the investigation. Its exports to the United States increased 42% in the first eight months of this year compared with the corresponding period in 2025, making it the US trading partner with the largest goods surplus, ahead of China and Mexico. At the end of 2025, Vietnam ranked fourth.
The increase has strengthened Vietnam’s importance in US import supply chains, while also bringing greater attention to the trade imbalance and the country’s role in manufacturing goods destined for the American market.
While major manufacturers and retailers have warned against additional tariffs, several US industry groups have called for penalties, arguing that Vietnamese producers benefit from unfair trade practices.
Organizations representing American steel, seafood, plywood, solar panel and wood product manufacturers accused Vietnam of unfair practices and urged the administration to impose new duties.
Intellectual property organizations have also pressed Washington to secure stronger commitments from Hanoi to tackle piracy and improve enforcement. Their submissions point to concerns involving software licensing, online distribution of copyrighted films and television programmes, and access for legitimate content providers.
The Business Software Alliance, whose members include Microsoft, Oracle and IBM, said about three-quarters of software installed on personal computers in Vietnam was unlicensed. It cited a 2017 survey and criticized what it described as inadequate enforcement, arguing that repeated Vietnamese commitments had not sufficiently addressed the problem.
The Motion Picture Association described Vietnam as a major center for online piracy. It said websites hosted in the country that distribute unauthorized films and television programmes attracted more than 12.5 billion visits worldwide last year.
The association called for stronger enforcement against piracy and improved market access for legitimate streaming services.
The competing submissions expose the difficulty facing Washington as it considers how to address intellectual property concerns without imposing costs on American companies that depend on Vietnamese manufacturing. Technology companies and retailers have an interest in maintaining access to production networks, while domestic producers and copyright holders are seeking measures they believe would protect their businesses from unfair competition and unauthorized distribution.
The outcome could also influence the broader US-Vietnam trade relationship. With Vietnam now running a larger goods surplus with the United States than China or Mexico, the administration faces pressure to address trade and intellectual property concerns while managing the potential consequences for American importers and manufacturers.
The November 29 deadline will provide a key point in the investigation, although the submissions do not establish whether Washington will impose additional tariffs, which sectors could be affected, or how any new duties would interact with the existing 12.5% levy.

high_priority_articles.summary: OCBC: Markets can absorb a 25-bps Fed rate hike  IDNFinancials
high_priority_articles.full_text:
JAKARTA - PT Bank OCBC NISP Tbk (NISP) has urged investors to monitor developments in US inflation, as these could influence the Federal Reserve's (The Fed) interest rate policy, capital flows and exchange rates in emerging markets, including the rupiah.
OCBC Group Chief Economist and Head of Research Selena Ling said US inflation was one of the key indicators investors should watch amid global economic uncertainty.
"Inflation will determine how long interest rates remain elevated. This, in turn, will affect capital flows, exchange rates, including the rupiah, as well as financing costs for businesses and households," Selena said at an OCBC media briefing in Jakarta on Tuesday (3 November).
According to her, markets expect the Fed could still raise interest rates by 25 basis points at its December 2026 meeting. However, the direction of monetary policy beyond that decision will depend on inflation developments.
Selena believes markets could still adjust if the Fed raises rates by just 25 basis points in December and subsequently keeps them unchanged for an extended period.
Conversely, more aggressive rate increases extending into 2027 could place greater pressure on global financial markets, particularly emerging economies.
Beyond US inflation, investors should also monitor geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and Ukraine. Prolonged conflicts could keep energy prices elevated and increase uncertainty across global supply chains.
Selena said these uncertainties meant investors needed to prepare strategies to manage various risks that could occur simultaneously, a phenomenon known as a polycrisis.
In such conditions, investors are advised to maintain liquidity and diversify their portfolios to reduce asset concentration risks.
"Investors need to remain flexible, maintain sufficient liquidity for future needs, while continuing to invest and seek opportunities," she said.
Diversification can be achieved across different asset classes, industry sectors, markets and currencies. This strategy is considered helpful in managing risks while maintaining flexibility as market conditions change.
Selena also cautioned investors against making decisions based on short-term market volatility. Asset allocation should be aligned with each investor's financial objectives, risk profile and investment horizon.
These global risks are also a concern for businesses. Selena believes companies need to strengthen supply chain resilience by reassessing their suppliers, target markets and business partners.
According to her, companies can no longer rely solely on just-in-time strategies, which focus on timely deliveries. They also need to establish alternative supply arrangements through a just-in-case approach to anticipate potential disruptions.
Meanwhile, Selena highlighted the sustainability of the artificial intelligence (AI) investment cycle. Several Asian countries are integrated into the semiconductor, data centre and cloud computing supply chains that support the global AI industry.
However, an investment slowdown in these sectors could affect economic growth, revenues and job creation in countries dependent on AI supply chains.
For Indonesia, Selena said economic resilience was also supported by adequate foreign exchange reserves. The country's reserves stood at US$146.3 billion at the end of September 2026, equivalent to 5.3 months of imports.
She added that fiscal discipline and the government's ability to maintain macroeconomic stability were crucial to sustaining investor confidence amid global volatility.
Selena stressed that investors should maintain a long-term strategy while ensuring adequate liquidity and adjusting their portfolios to match their individual risk tolerance. (DH/LM)

high_priority_articles.title: Kazimir Warns of Further ECB Rate Hikes as Digital Euro Plans Advance - Coin Edition

- Kazimir warns that persistent inflation could require further ECB interest rate hikes.
- Rising energy and food prices, alongside a weaker euro, could increase inflationary pressure.
- The ECB plans to launch a 12-month digital euro pilot in the second half of 2027.
Slovakia’s central bank chief Peter Kazimir warned on November 2 that persistently high inflation could require the European Central Bank (ECB) to raise interest rates further, suggesting that markets may be underestimating the monetary tightening needed to bring inflation back to target.
Separately, the ECB announced on October 30 that it had selected two technology and telecommunications groups to provide network services for its digital euro project, marking another step toward testing the proposed central bank digital currency.
Kazimir Warns Inflation Could Require Further Rate Hikes
In a separate statement on November 2, Slovakia’s central bank chief Peter Kazimir warned that the ECB’s recent decision to hold interest rates steady should not be viewed as the end of monetary tightening. He cited persistent energy price pressures, rising food prices, and a weaker exchange rate that makes imports more expensive.
Kazimir said rising costs could eventually spread through the economy as businesses pass higher expenses on to consumers. He also warned that inflation expectations could shift before broader price pressures become visible in official data.
The ECB’s next policy decision is expected in December, when policymakers will have access to updated forecasts and additional economic information. Kazimir did not specify the number or size of any potential rate increases. However, he said markets might be underestimating how much further tightening would be needed to bring inflation back to the ECB’s target and keep it there.
For financial markets, the comments signal that interest-rate expectations could change if inflation remains persistent. However, the digital euro project and monetary policy decisions follow separate processes. Progress on the digital euro’s legislation and infrastructure should therefore be monitored independently of developments that could influence the ECB’s interest-rate decisions.
ECB Selects Two Digital Euro Network Groups
The ECB announced on October 30 that it had selected two groups to provide network services for the digital euro project.
The first group involves Nexi Payments and Deutsche Telekom Business Solutions. Their contract entered into force on September 28 and will initially provide connectivity for the digital euro pilot. The second group consists of Telefónica and Indra’s technology arm, Minsait. Its contract will start in May 2027.
The ECB’s official announcement states that both groups will connect participating payment service providers and national central banks to the digital euro service platform and enable communication between its components.
Both network providers will be ready as of 2029 to provide connectivity services for a potential digital euro issuance. Payment service providers will be able to choose either network to connect to the digital euro platform, subject to the ECB Governing Council’s decision on the project’s next phase.
Digital Euro Pilot Planned for 2027
The ECB intends to launch a 12-month pilot in the second half of 2027. Thirty-six selected payment service providers will participate in testing payments and assessing the system’s technical and operational capabilities.
However, the selection of network providers and the planned pilot do not constitute final approval for issuing the digital euro. The ECB has stated that a decision on issuance will only be made after the relevant European legislation is adopted and the Governing Council makes its decision. The pilot will help test the system and assess its readiness ahead of that decision.
The ECB is moving ahead with its digital euro preparations, while Kazimir’s warning puts the eurozone’s inflation outlook and potential rate hikes back in focus.

high_priority_articles.title: NCSC Chief Warns of Imminent AI Ransomware Threat to UK Critical Infrastructure - Infosecurity Magazine
high_priority_articles.summary: NCSC Chief Warns of Imminent AI Ransomware Threat to UK Critical Infrastructure  Infosecurity Magazine
high_priority_articles.full_text:
AI-powered malware is strongly expected to feature in ransomware attacks on the UK’s critical national infrastructure by 2028, the country’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has warned.
The country faces “a real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents,” NCSC CEO Richard Horne said during the launch event for the agency’s annual State of the Cyber Nation report in London, on November 3.
Horne said this heightened threat is supercharged by the use of AI, whose impact “will be felt by us all, whether you and your organization choose to harness it or not.”
The report warned that AI-powered malicious software is “highly likely” to be used in cyber-attacks conducted by financially motivated hackers against the UK’s power stations, airports and hospitals by 2028.
It also warned that nation states including Russia and China will routinely use AI in their cyber activity to achieve their geopolitical goals.
Yet, Horne emphasized that AI-based threats have not fundamentally revealed anything new.
The risk that looms is “not because AI has invented new ways to attack us,” he argued, but “because vulnerabilities that have been tolerated for far too long can now be discovered and exploited at a scale that was once unimaginable.”
He pointed to “far too many organizations” relying on “tech on the cheap.”
“End-of-life systems kept running for just one more year, well-needed upgrades pushed back, as a 'cost efficiency' and technology providers failing to invest in security by design and default,” Horne outlined.
“We have installed technology then failed to invest in it throughout its lifecycle. Granted access where it was convenient rather than where it was necessary. Procured services based solely on their price without asking whether the technologies and operations underpinning them was resilient or secure. And failed to put in place the monitoring needed to detect when things go wrong,” he added.
UK Government Announces New Cybersecurity Investments
The best recent example, Horne said, is the threat of the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. He noted that his agency has issued 110,000 proactive notifications and Early Warning alerts to UK organizations in response to the PHP vulnerabilities.
He also welcomed recent news that the British government has invested £60m ($80.4m) into developing the first phase of a national Cyber Shield, including a £25m ($33.5m) Challenge Fund supporting UK AI and cyber security innovators, and £70m ($93.8m) for a new National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre.
These announcements, made on October 24, come alongside an additional £120m ($160.8m) investment in the AI Security Institute (AISI) and the establishment of new AI Cyber Security Centre of Excellence, ran by the NCSC in Manchester to provide world leading AI security expertise within government.
The government has also committed £40m ($53.6m) to establishing a National Agentic Security Unit to monitor and respond to uncontrolled AI bots, alongside a further £24m ($32.1m) to strengthen public-sector cyber defenses using advanced AI technology.
Alongside these investments, Cyber Security Minister, Baroness Lloyd, announced in a speech at the NCSC Annual Review event that the UK government is offering a 75% discount on Cyber Essentials certification for micro, small and medium-sized businesses, bringing the cost down to between £80 ($107) and £125 ($168), plus VAT.
More than 230 businesses have also signed up to the government's Cyber Resilience Pledge, which will allow participating organizations to refer SMEs in their supply chains for free Cyber Essentials certification, with selected businesses also receiving support from a free cyber security advisor.
The government also announced 14 new Software Security Ambassadors, including Fortinet, Thales, Capgemini and Zscaler, which will work with the government to promote secure software development and encourage wider adoption of its Software Security Code of Practice.
A “Moment of Choice” for UK Organizations
Horne said UK organizations and at “a moment of choice” and urged them to “reckon with the current state of their cybersecurity” as new technologies like AI will expose vulnerabilities, failings and underinvestment at an unprecedented speed and scale in the years ahead.
The NCSC report also suggested that the UK is at a point of “enormous consequence” for cybersecurity and that organizations must make use of the tools, standards and frameworks that already exist and are evidenced to protect them from conventional and AI-powered cyber-attacks.
"We can be a nation where leaders of all organizations actively choose to invest with urgency and where all organizations make security and resilience a fundamental requirement, not an afterthought. The collective result would be a source of enduring national strength for us all,” Horne said in his speech.
He added that failing to make these choices will result in leaders “having to look their investors, shareholders, employees, customers, suppliers, in the eye and explain, when food isn’t on shelves, lights aren’t on, businesses have gone under.”
Commenting on the report, Anthony Young, CEO at UK-based critical infrastructure security provider Bridewell, stressed that the NCSC’s two-year warning “feels generous.”
“AI is already helping attackers, and vulnerability discovery is accelerating faster than many organizations can test and deploy patches. There is no time to wait when so many of the weaknesses attackers can exploit are already there, highlighting the recent attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems are a good example of this and “an extension of the problems we have seen for years with internet-connected CCTV and heating or ventilation systems.”
“Organizations cannot assume that insurance will resolve the consequences of an attack when essential services are disrupted. Cyber Essentials matters because so many attacks still exploit basic weaknesses, and leaving those weaknesses in place makes life too easy for everyone from amateur hackers to nation-state attackers. We’ve spent 25 years telling organisations to get the basics right. AI is making it harder for them to get away with ignoring that advice,” Young added.
The warnings come as the UK government is taking action through the introduction of the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill and the forthcoming National Cyber Action Plan to strengthen the UK's defenses.

high_priority_articles.title: NCSC Warns AI Could Accelerate Ransomware Attacks on Critical Infrastructure - CyberSecurityNews
high_priority_articles.summary: NCSC Warns AI Could Accelerate Ransomware Attacks on Critical Infrastructure  CyberSecurityNews
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The UK’s National Cyber Security Center handled 80 nationally significant cyber incidents during its latest reporting year, warning that artificial intelligence is making attacks faster, cheaper and easier to carry out. Its 2026 Annual Review records 1,831 attack reports, with 337 incidents requiring support from its Incident Management Team.
The review covers 1 September 2025 to 31 August 2026, marking the NCSC’s tenth year as part of GCHQ. Published on November 3, the NCSC Annual Review 2026 warns that AI is increasing pressure on organizations still struggling to fix known security weaknesses.
The 80 nationally significant incidents represent a subset of the 337 cases that needed NCSC support, not the total number of cyber attacks across the UK. Alongside its response work, the agency notified 8,500 organizations of events indicating suspected system compromise through its Early Warning service.
The NCSC cautions against reading incident totals as a simple measure of whether threats are rising or falling. Reporting levels vary, major incidents can influence annual figures, and early alerts may prevent smaller compromises from developing into cases requiring national support. Response complexity also differs widely between incidents.
That context matters when comparing this review with earlier reporting on nationally significant UK cyber attacks. A lower incident count does not, by itself, prove that organizations face less risk or that the impact of individual attacks has decreased.
AI Could Accelerate Ransomware
The report’s central finding is not that attackers have abandoned established techniques. Instead, AI is helping them research targets, produce convincing social engineering messages, discover software flaws, and develop exploit code more efficiently. Skilled operators currently gain the greatest benefit because they can check results and correct mistakes.
The agency’s incident management findings draw an important line between observed activity and future risks. Its responders have begun seeing attackers use AI tools, but none of those observed uses enabled a new class of attack. Existing security controls therefore remain directly relevant.
Across the large organizations covered by its incident data, 88% of incidents involved four initial access routes: public-facing applications, phishing, valid accounts and external remote services. These findings show why exposed software, stolen login details and poorly protected remote access remain immediate concerns, even as AI capabilities improve.
Human involvement also remains important. The NCSC assesses that attackers will continue using AI mainly to improve existing operations rather than routinely handing complete attacks to autonomous systems. Operators still need to direct tools, validate findings and adapt when an approach fails.
The review warns that AI-powered malware is highly likely to feature in a ransomware attack against UK critical national infrastructure between now and 2028. This is a forecast, not confirmation that such an incident has already happened.
Its assessment of threats to the UK also expects China, Russia and other states to routinely use AI cyber capabilities by 2028. The likely result is an increase in the speed and scale of sophisticated operations against UK targets.
Businesses face risks from their own AI adoption too. The report warns that employees using unapproved AI services can expose sensitive company information and leave employers unable to track how that data is handled. Earlier coverage of CISA and NCSC secure AI development guidance explains why security must be considered throughout an AI system’s life.
For defenders, AI-assisted flaw discovery could create a growing workload of security updates. The NCSC urges organisations to prepare for a “patch wave” by improving their ability to deploy fixes quickly, frequently and across suppliers. Not every AI-discovered flaw will be exploitable, but delays can give attackers opportunities.
The immediate priorities remain practical: maintain an accurate view of systems, patch exposed services, control account access, protect backups and rehearse incident response. The review also supports wider passkey adoption and better understanding of supplier dependencies. These measures address the access routes responders continue to encounter.
AI can also help defenders identify weaknesses, review alerts, and support faster response. However, automated actions need clear limits and human oversight to avoid disruption. The challenge is turning that potential into reliable protection while replacing aging technology and consistently applying the basic controls that many organizations still lack today.
