high_priority_articles.title: Fintech associations from 12 countries, the EBA, and ASEAN regulators build a new financial corridor in Kuala Lumpur - Singapore Business Review
high_priority_articles.summary: Fintech associations from 12 countries, the EBA, and ASEAN regulators build a new financial corridor in Kuala Lumpur  Singapore Business Review
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Finweek Kuala Lumpur is where European capital meets ASEAN velocity.
The global financial axis is shifting. Whilst Europe has built the world’s most comprehensive regulatory architecture with MiCA and digital finance frameworks, ASEAN is driving the world’s fastest-growing digital economy. On Wednesday, 11 November 2026, the two regions will stop talking about cooperation in theory and start building shared market infrastructure in practice.
At the Founding Edition of Finweek Kuala Lumpur 2026, the premier EU–ASEAN institutional fintech summit, the national fintech associations of twelve countries will take the main stage to sign the Founding Memorandum of the EU–ASEAN Investment Gateway.
Convened by Finweek Global, the organiser, together with Fintech Valley Europe as co-organiser and in partnership with the International Digital Economies Association (IDEA)—which spans 100 countries—endorsed by the European Digital Finance Association (EDFA) as the European network, and joined by the Global FinTech Alliance (GFA), the coalition unites national associations from Slovakia (FINAS), Czechia, Hungary, Ukraine, Moldova (Fintech Moldova) and Armenia (FinTech Armenia, together with FinTech EurAsia) with their counterparts across Indonesia (AFSI, Asosiasi Blockchain Indonesia), Myanmar (MDEA, FinTech Alliance Myanmar), Cambodia (CAFT), Vietnam (APAC DAO / Vietnam Fintech Summit), the Philippines and Malaysia, the host nation. Together, they represent thousands of financial technology innovators across Europe, ASEAN, and Eurasia.
A sovereign gateway for capital and regulation
Finweek Kuala Lumpur is not a conventional commercial event—it is a B2G and B2B diplomatic platform designed to turn regulatory alignment into cross-border deal flow.
At the heart of the summit is the Regulators’ Table, chaired by Kati Ferry (CEO, EUROCHAM Malaysia). Inside one room, senior policymakers and supervisors from the European Banking Authority (EBA — Rūta Merkevičiūtė, Head of the Digital Finance Unit), the Ministry of Finance of the Slovak Republic (Martin Peter, Director of the Banking Department), Otoritas Jasa Keuangan (OJK) of Indonesia (R. Rinto, Director, Digital Services and Cybersecurity Specialist Group), the Labuan Financial Services Authority (Labuan FSA — Doreen Fadli, Acting Director, Market Development & Innovations), the Trust Regulator of Cambodia (Sakal Ney, Deputy Director General) and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) of the Philippines will address the hard operational realities of cross-border finance: real-world asset (RWA) tokenisation, the practical lessons of Europe’s MiCA framework, cross-border settlement, and stablecoin supervision.
Diplomatic momentum carries onto the main stage as the Ambassadors of the Czech Republic (H.E. Juraj Koudelka), Hungary (H.E. Dr Sándor Sipos), and Ukraine (H.E. Dr Hennadii Nadolenko), alongside senior diplomatic representatives of the Embassy of Indonesia and the Embassy of the Slovak Republic, officially open the afternoon Corridor block.
“Fintech no longer needs just founders; it needs diplomats,” said Davy Čajko, Founder of Finweek, President of FINAS (Fintech & Insurtech Association of Slovakia), and architect of the EU–ASEAN corridor. “Europe brings deep institutional capital and regulatory clarity through MiCA. ASEAN brings unmatched demographic energy, rapid adoption, and scale. Yet until today, a founder or investor crossing between our regions had to navigate fragmented rules alone. On 11 November, we are putting European and ASEAN regulators, ambassadors, and the associations of twelve countries into one room—not to exchange business cards, but to sign a joint commitment, announce the Malaysia Fintech Radar partnership, and open a Sovereign Gateway for capital and talent.”
The Malaysia Fintech Radar: A research partnership announced
To move capital across borders, institutional investors need verified data, not just stage panels. A flagship milestone of the Founding Edition (16:40 MYT) is the announcement of the research partnership behind the Malaysia Fintech Radar, presented by Dr Masrina Nadia Mohd Salleh of Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia (UKM).
Five pillars of the main stage (11 November 2026)
Instead of generic keynotes, the summit’s confirmed leaders focus on what actually runs in production:
Cyber Sovereignty & The ASEAN Investment Thesis (09:30–10:25): Following opening remarks by Davy Čajko and Kati Ferry (EUROCHAM Malaysia), YBhg. Dato’ Ts. Dr Haji Amirudin Abdul Wahab (Special Advisor on Cybersecurity & Digital Technology to HH The Crown Prince of Selangor; former CEO, CyberSecurity Malaysia) delivers the opening keynote on digital sovereignty and cyber resilience. The investment fireside follows with Farah Jaafar (Straits Investment Bank), Nicholas Kew (Crewstone International), and Dr Bilal İlhan (Presidency of the Republic of Türkiye Investment and Finance Office).
AI in Financial Operations — From Pilots to Accountability (10:45): Moderated by Firuz Alimov (The AI Collective), bringing together policy architects and front-line operators: Sam Majid (Former CEO, National AI Office Malaysia), Dr Aini Suzana Ariffin (Industrial Institute of Responsible AI), Dr Sekar Jaganathan (Kenanga Investment Bank), Lolitta Suffian (Bank Simpanan Nasional), Nate Wentzlaff (FinanTEXT, USA), and Eddy Wong Kok Hoe (VSure).
Islamic Digital Finance at Scale & The ASEAN–GCC–EU Nexus (11:35): Chaired by Aida Lim Abdullah (MFPC), examining sukuk tokenisation and Shariah-compliant digital assets with Vikra Ijas (AFSI Indonesia), Prof Irfan Syauqi Beik (IPB University), Effendy Zulkifly (YAPEIM Holdings), and Muttmaein Zairul (Masryef Advisory).
Tokenisation, RWA & Cross-Border Stablecoins (14:10–16:25): Featuring an opening industry case by Tran Hung (CEO, Uquid), a regulatory keynote on the MiCA gateway by Martin Peter (Ministry of Finance of the Slovak Republic), and the flagship Tokenisation panel with Michael Heaney (EY Malaysia), Krishnavenee Krishnan (KLDX), Jason Ding (MHub / Malaysia Proptech Association), and Shinoy Varghese (S&P Global Ratings). At 15:35, Gerard M. Pillai (PIKOM) leads the cross-border payments and stablecoin debate with Razin Nizar (Pragmax Consulting), Muhammad Yusuf Musa (Nanovest / Asosiasi Blockchain Indonesia), Edison Tan (EMAS ESTATE) and Harpreet Singh (Access Blockchain).
The Founding Circle, Corridor Showcase & Startup Pitch (12:30 & 16:50–18:10): High-growth startups including GORO, Koha Digital, and GoBarakah pitch to an international investor jury (Vatsala Arunachalam, Karen S Puah, Ben Stubbings, Audra Pakalnytė, Dr Alexander Titov). In the afternoon, Cristina Amor Maclang (IDEA / Global FinTech Alliance) chairs the Founding Circle townhall with association presidents and a message from Alessandra Guion, Chair of the Board of the European Digital Finance Association (EDFA), followed by Tan Sri Michael Yeoh (President, KSI Strategic Institute for Asia Pacific) chairing the Corridor Showcase with Dr Zsolt Polereczki (Neuron Labs) and Matthew Barsing (ASEAN Rising), culminating in the 17:50 Signing Ceremony and the Founding Dinner.
Landing Day in TRX (Thursday, 12 November 2026)
Because market entry happens on the ground, Landing Day takes visiting European delegations, regulators, and investors out of the ballroom and directly into Tun Razak Exchange (TRX), Malaysia’s international financial district—starting at INFINITY8 Reserve TRX (The Mastermind Mansion, Level 23)—to connect directly with licensing authorities, innovation hubs, and financial institutions where European companies establish their ASEAN headquarters.
Building on European momentum
The Kuala Lumpur Founding Edition follows the milestone 10th anniversary edition of Finweek Bratislava (13–14 October 2026), which welcomed 81 speakers from 15 countries, more than 400 registrations from 26 countries, and six public authorities—where H.E. Dato’ Fenny Nuli, Ambassador of Malaysia in Vienna, inaugurated the Europe–Asia corridor dialogue.
Registration, partnerships, and media accreditation

US Trade Representative Ambassador Jamieson Greer confirmed President Donald Trump’s decision, stating that the administrations in Pretoria and Kigali are engaging in practices that violate the eligibility requirements of the landmark trade programme. The termination shuts the two African economies out of preferential access to the US market, marking one of the most significant diplomatic and economic ruptures between Washington and sub-Saharan Africa in recent years.
AGOA, enacted in 2000, has long served as the cornerstone of US economic engagement with Africa, allowing eligible sub-Saharan countries to export thousands of products duty-free to the United States. To maintain this status, beneficiary nations must meet strict criteria, including establishing market-based economies, the rule of law, political pluralism, and the elimination of barriers to US trade and investment. They must also protect human rights and avoid activities that undermine US national security or foreign policy interests.
Legal mechanisms and diplomatic friction
The legal mechanism for this expulsion relies on the executive authority granted to the US President under the original AGOA legislation. The law explicitly requires the President to monitor the progress of beneficiary countries and empowers the executive to withdraw designation if a country is not making continual progress in meeting the eligibility criteria. By formally declaring that both nations are engaging in inconsistent practices, Ambassador Greer has initiated the statutory withdrawal process, which mandates a consultation period with the US Congress before the termination becomes irrevocable.
While the US government has not released an exhaustive public dossier detailing every infraction, the Trump administration’s concerns regarding Rwanda primarily centre on human rights abuses and restrictions on political freedom. Kigali has faced sustained criticism from international rights organisations over the suppression of political opposition and the alleged transnational repression of dissidents.
For South Africa, the friction is largely rooted in its foreign policy alignments and trade disputes. Pretoria has drawn intense scrutiny from Washington over its diplomatic posture, particularly its relations with US geopolitical adversaries and its stance on various international conflicts. Furthermore, South Africa has faced ongoing trade irritants, including disputes over poultry tariffs and access for US agricultural producers, which Washington has repeatedly argued violate the spirit of AGOA’s market-access provisions.
Economic fallout for export sectors
The economic consequences of the expulsion will be immediate and severe for both nations once the January 2027 deadline takes effect. South Africa is arguably the most sophisticated beneficiary of AGOA, using the preferential access to build a robust export pipeline, particularly in the automotive and agricultural sectors. The automotive industry, which relies heavily on duty-free access to export vehicles to the US, faces the prospect of suddenly being subjected to standard Most Favoured Nation (MFN) tariffs. These standard tariffs could render South African exports uncompetitive against rivals in Asia and Latin America, threatening thousands of manufacturing jobs in the Eastern Cape and Gauteng provinces.
Furthermore, Pretoria’s agricultural sector, which has battled sanitary and phytosanitary barriers to export citrus and stone fruit to the US, now faces the additional burden of import duties. Industry bodies have warned that the combined effect of non-tariff barriers and the sudden imposition of tariffs could devastate commercial farming operations that have oriented their supply chains toward the North American market.
Rwanda, though a smaller economy, has leveraged AGOA to develop a burgeoning apparel and textile manufacturing sector. The loss of duty-free quotas will likely trigger factory closures and job losses in a country that has aggressively positioned itself as a light-manufacturing hub for the region. Kigali had previously engaged in trade disputes with Washington over second-hand clothing imports, which resulted in the temporary suspension of its apparel benefits, making the broader termination a compounding economic blow.
Strategic recalibration of US-Africa trade
The decision underscores a shift in US trade policy under the current administration, which has increasingly prioritised strict bilateral compliance and geopolitical alignment over the broad-based developmental goals that historically underpinned AGOA. By wielding the threat and eventual execution of AGOA expulsion as a foreign policy tool, Washington is signalling that trade preferences are conditional on broader diplomatic cooperation and adherence to American strategic interests.
Regional economic blocs and trade analysts are now assessing the potential contagion effect. The expulsion of two of the continent's most prominent economies raises questions about the future stability of AGOA, which is currently undergoing its periodic renewal debates in the US Congress. African trade negotiators have long argued for a more predictable, long-term renewal of the pact to encourage fixed capital investment, but the politicisation of eligibility criteria introduces a new layer of uncertainty for investors operating across the continent. This uncertainty complicates the objectives of the African Continental Free Trade Area, as external market shocks force nations to recalibrate their industrialisation strategies without guaranteed access to their most lucrative overseas markets.
Trade unions and civil society organisations in South Africa have expressed alarm at the potential job losses, urging the government to urgently repair diplomatic relations with Washington. The termination represents a profound recalibration of US-Africa economic relations, prioritising strategic compliance over historical trade solidarity, and leaves both Pretoria and Kigali with a narrow window to engage in high-level diplomatic interventions before the new year.

high_priority_articles.title: Ethiopia: Will Renewed Conflict Derail Ethiopia's Economic Growth? - allAfrica.com
high_priority_articles.summary: Ethiopia: Will Renewed Conflict Derail Ethiopia's Economic Growth?  allAfrica.com
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Ethiopia's economy is growing strongly. But renewed fighting in the north of the BRICS member state could deter investment, strain public finances and push up the cost of living.
Ethiopia's economy is growing strongly. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) forecasts real growth of 9.2% for the 2025–26 fiscal year. But renewed fighting in the north, high reconstruction costs and climate-related crop problems are threatening the country's economic recovery.
London-based financial analyst Abdulmenan Mohammed warns of the consequences of further escalation. "If there is a major conflict [...] the current economic growth will not be sustainable," he told DW.
The costly legacy of the Tigray war
Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines
The war that raged in Tigray and other parts of Ethiopia between 2020 and 2022 inflicted extensive damage. Infrastructure was destroyed, businesses lost production capacity and agricultural land could no longer be cultivated in some areas.
A World Bank-backed damage and needs assessment puts the damage caused by several conflicts in Ethiopia between November 2020 and December 2021 at more than $22.6 billion (€20.2 billion). Economic losses amounted to around $6 billion. The estimated bill for reconstruction and economic recovery stands at approximately $19.7 billion, which covers the total funding needed, not annual costs or damage caused by the current escalation.
A reconstruction plan covered the period from 2023 to 2028. However, it remains uncertain whether the work can be fully funded and completed within that timeframe.
Financial analyst Abdulmenan Mohammed believes the economic consequences of the Tigray war were even more severe. In addition to the direct destruction, he points to lost economic output, high inflation and foreign currency shortages at the time. International trade conditions also deteriorated: in 2022, Ethiopia lost its benefits under the US African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), which had allowed certain African exports to enter the US market duty-free.
Growth despite the crisis
Following the Pretoria peace agreement in November 2022, the economy began to recover. According to the IMF, it grew by 7.2% in 2022–23 and 8.1% in 2023–24. The organization puts growth at 9.2% for 2024–25 and forecasts a further 9.2% for 2025–26. Agriculture, mining and electricity generation are among the main drivers.
This does not contradict the economic damage caused by the war. Gross domestic product (GDP) measures the total economic output of a country. If major sectors outside conflict-affected areas continue to expand, the overall economy can grow even while individual regions are still suffering the consequences of violence.
However, high growth rates do not mean that the country's economic problems have been resolved. Reconstruction remains a major challenge, inflation continues to put pressure on households and the government has to service its debt. In late 2023, Ethiopia defaulted after missing an interest payment on a Eurobond. Reforms supported by an IMF program launched in 2024 are intended to address structural weaknesses in the economy.
More military spending, less money for development
A renewed escalation could put additional pressure on public finances. The government would have to spend more on military personnel, equipment and logistics. At the same time, economic activity and, consequently, tax revenues could decline in the affected regions.
"A substantial share of government resources would be tied up in military spending that would otherwise be available for infrastructure, education and social services," warned Abdulmenan Mohammed. The extent of this impact would depend on the scale and duration of any renewed conflict.A prolonged war could also prompt businesses to postpone investments. International lenders and donors might become more cautious, while the government would need additional funds for security and humanitarian assistance. This could leave less money available for roads, energy infrastructure and other development projects.
Inflation and foreign currency shortages
The IMF forecasts an average inflation rate of 11.7% for 2025–26. Prices are therefore expected to continue rising, although at a slower pace than in previous years.
Abdulmenan Mohammed expects a further escalation to intensify inflationary pressures. "If the conflict escalates further, inflation is likely to rise," he said. To finance additional spending, the government might resort to more domestic borrowing. This could crowd out private businesses by making it harder for them to access credit and finance investments.
The military also needs foreign currency to purchase equipment from abroad. If this demand increases, fewer foreign exchange reserves could be available to private businesses for imports. This would put further pressure on the birr exchange rate and drive up the cost of imported goods, fuel and industrial inputs.
The extent of these effects on the BRICS member state would also depend on export earnings, monetary policy and developments in international markets. A new surge in inflation is therefore a risk, but not an inevitable consequence of the escalation. A combination of rising prices and uncertain incomes would be particularly difficult for poorer households.
Agriculture and tourism particularly vulnerable
Abdulmenan Mohammed sees agriculture, as well as the tourism and hospitality sectors, as particularly vulnerable. "Agriculture is especially exposed because much of the fighting takes place in rural areas where farmers work," he said.
Insecurity around farmland, disrupted transport routes and shortages of agricultural inputs can undermine production. At the same time, parts of the country are experiencing insufficient rainfall and poor harvest prospects. Failed harvests reduce farmers' incomes, while lower food supplies can push prices even higher.
Tourism is also highly sensitive to security risks. Travel advisories and reports of fighting can deter visitors, reducing revenues for hotels and tour operators.
Could neighboring countries benefit from the crisis?
When making investment decisions, international investors consider not only market size but also political stability, security and the reliability of state institutions. A further escalation could therefore delay investment decisions or prompt companies to consider alternative locations.
However, there is currently no concrete evidence that companies are already withdrawing investments from Ethiopia because of the fighting and relocating them to neighboring countries such as Kenya. Abdulmenan Mohammed also sees no demonstrable economic advantage for Kenya at this stage. Beyond security, factors such as tax administration, public services and governance also play a decisive role.

high_priority_articles.title: Tajikistan faces growing risks from dependence on labor migration, report warns - Азия-Плюс
high_priority_articles.summary: Tajikistan faces growing risks from dependence on labor migration, report warns  Азия-Плюс
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Labor migration helps Tajikistan ease unemployment and support household incomes, but maintaining migration at its current scale could become increasingly difficult in the long term, according to a new report by the Eurasian Fund for Stabilization and Development (EFSD).
The report, titled Economic Growth, Demographics and the Labor Market: Realities and Challenges, was presented on October 29 at the international economic conference Toward Balanced Economic Development in Astana.
According to the report, labor migration remains one of Tajikistan’s main mechanisms for easing pressure on its domestic labor market. With the national economy unable to generate enough jobs for everyone seeking employment, many citizens look for work abroad.
Money sent home by migrant workers helps sustain household consumption, reduce poverty and stimulate domestic demand.
The report notes that remittances have reached the equivalent of nearly half of Tajikistan’s gross domestic product (GDP) in some periods, making it one of the world’s most remittance-dependent economies.
Why does dependence on migration pose risks?
EFSD experts warn that changes in the migration policies of destination countries could make it increasingly difficult for Tajik citizens to find employment abroad.
Russia remains the main destination for Tajik labor migrants. However, tighter migration regulations are limiting the Russian labor market’s ability to absorb foreign workers.
Kazakhstan also attracts workers from neighboring countries, but its labor market remains considerably smaller than Russia’s in terms of employment opportunities for migrants.
Heavy reliance on earnings from abroad also creates challenges for Tajikistan’s domestic economy.
According to the researchers, while remittances boost household spending and imports, they do not necessarily lead to increased domestic production or the creation of more productive, better-paid jobs.
Migration may also discourage some workers from pursuing vocational education and professional training, particularly when jobs available abroad require relatively few qualifications.
Tajikistan’s working-age population to grow by 2.46 million
Demographic trends are expected to put additional pressure on Tajikistan’s labor market over the coming years.
According to EFSD projections, the country’s working-age population, defined as people aged 15–64, will increase from 6.34 million in 2025 to 8.8 million by 2040.
This represents an increase of 2.46 million people over 15 years, potentially creating substantial additional demand for jobs.
EFSD experts argue that Tajikistan cannot rely on labor migration alone to address its employment challenges.
They recommend expanding domestic employment opportunities, supporting private sector development, creating more productive jobs and improving workforce skills.
How dependent is Tajikistan on labor migration?
World Bank data illustrate the scale of Tajikistan’s dependence on money earned abroad.
In 2025, remittances were equivalent to approximately 46% of the country’s GDP, compared with 39% in 2023 and around 49% in 2024.
An estimated one-quarter of Tajikistan’s workforce travels abroad in search of employment.
One of the main drivers of labor migration is the substantial wage gap between Tajikistan and destination countries.
According to the Agency for Statistics under the President of Tajikistan, the average monthly wage in the country stood at 3,508 somoni in July 2026.
The World Bank estimates that Tajik migrants working in Russia can earn at least three times as much as they would in comparable jobs at home, even in relatively low-skilled occupations.
Such dependence leaves Tajikistan vulnerable to developments in Russia’s labor market. Fewer job opportunities, stricter migration regulations or declining migrant earnings could reduce remittance inflows, putting pressure on household incomes and domestic consumption.

high_priority_articles.full_text:
The Saudi-led coalition against the Houthis said it intercepted a drone over the Mecca region following a series of attacks by the Iran-backed militants against the kingdom.
"Interception and destruction of a drone in the Mecca region," Turki al-Malki, the coalition's spokesperson wrote on social media, without elaborating on the source of the attack.
The interception came a day after the coalition said that it had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile and two drones fired by the Houthis toward Saudi territory.
Mecca is home to one of Islam's holiest sites, the Kabba, which draws millions of pilgrims every year, making it a red line for Saudi Arabia and the Muslim world in general.
The development follows escalating hostilities between the Houthi group and the Saudi-led coalition, which supports Yemen's internationally recognized government.
Earlier Tuesday, the Houthis claimed that Saudi strikes had killed 17 civilians over two days this week.
The Houthi Health Ministry said in a statement that most of the people killed were children, "which shows that Saudi aircraft are targeting homes, residential neighborhoods and markets."
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said Monday evening that Riyadh had carried out "109 strikes over the past 24 hours" in Yemen, targeting the governorates of Saada, Taiz, Lahj, al-Jawf and Hodeidah.
The group also claimed drone attacks on Saudi airports in the east and south of the kingdom.
Yemen has been beset by war since 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa, with a Saudi-led coalition entering the conflict a year later in support of the government.
A 2022 truce fell apart in July and, in September, the Houthis launched an offensive to capture the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, which links Europe to Asia via the Red Sea and Suez Canal.
The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed in the impoverished country.

high_priority_articles.title: Grève du 5 novembre : entre lycéens, étudiants, syndicats de salariés et « gilets jaunes », le pari d’une convergence des mobilisations
high_priority_articles.summary: Alors que les mouvements de jeunes ont demandé un relais du monde du travail, les organisations syndicales ont appelé à défiler et à cesser le travail, jeudi, dans toute la France. Parmi les revendications : la revalorisation des salaires, la sauvegarde des services publics et la défense du droit de manifester.
high_priority_articles.full_text:
La date a été fixée longtemps à l’avance. Le 5 octobre, soit six jours après une journée d’action dans la fonction publique et alors que la contestation lycéenne prenait son envol, cinq syndicats de salariés (CFDT, CGT, FO, FSU, UNSA) ont appelé à défiler et à cesser le travail, jeudi 5 novembre. Leurs mots d’ordre sont larges : revalorisation du smic, ouverture « immédiate » de négociations sur les rémunérations, sauvegarde des services publics, de l’emploi et de l’industrie, justice fiscale par la taxation des gros patrimoines…
Depuis, la fronde dans l’enseignement secondaire s’est élargie aux universités et a connu une ampleur historique, se muant en un mouvement social qui embarque de multiples catégories : élèves, étudiants, travailleurs du privé et du public, anciens et nouveaux « gilets jaunes », parents et citoyens choqués par la brutalité des interventions policières à l’encontre des lycéens, notamment.
Après les trois « actes » des 17, 24 et 31 octobre contre – entre autres revendications – la vie chère, le rendez-vous de jeudi change de dimension : « Ça doit être une grande journée de convergence », a martelé, le 2 novembre, Sophie Binet, la secrétaire générale de la CGT, sur France 2. Fatigués par plus d’un mois de luttes, des lycéens le répètent : ils ont « besoin du relais » « du monde du travail ». Depuis que l’appel à manifester et à faire grève a été diffusé, trois autres organisations ont décidé de s’y associer : la CFTC, Solidaires et la CFE-CGC.

high_priority_articles.full_text:
Russia on Tuesday confirmed that peace talks with Ukraine and the U.S. will go ahead next week in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, while also signaling that a meeting between Presidents Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping to end the conflict was on the table.
Putin aide Vladimir Medinsky will serve as Moscow's chief negotiator at the talks in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on a conference call, according to Reuters.
Separately, first lady Melania Trump will bring Russian and Ukrainian representatives to the White House to discuss the local ceasefire in Kherson, the White House said Tuesday.
Monday saw the end of a six-day ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky and surrounding areas in the Kherson region to allow for evacuation of residents, in a pause of hostilities that the White House said was brokered by the first lady.
Ukraine on Monday accused Russia of using the ceasefire to reinforce its military positions in the city.
The first lady's summit on Thursday will be "an extraordinary moment in American history," the White House said, but did not name the representatives who will attend. Melania Trump will deliver remarks on the Oleshky ceasefire at 11 a.m. ET on Thursday, it added.
Peskov also said Tuesday the Kremlin hopes to finalize plans for a trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, the U.S. and China in the coming days. The comments follow earlier reports that these countries were planning to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine, without Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the table.
Zelenskyy has said that any negotiations over Ukraine's future must include Kyiv.
"It can be acceptable only when we are at the table of negotiations," he said on Oct. 20, adding that he had discussed the proposal of a three-way meeting between the U.S., China and Russia to negotiate an end to the nearly five-year full-scale war. "Nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine," he said.
Tensions between the U.S. and Ukraine have mounted over recent weeks amid continued strikes between Moscow and Kyiv, including on civilian and energy targets.
A series of moves by the Trump administration in October raised questions about Washington's reliability as Kyiv's most important military partner.
Tuesday's announcement follows U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff saying late Monday that Washington will mediate Ukraine-Russia peace talks in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11, focusing on security arrangements, de-escalation and humanitarian issues.
Witkoff also said that U.S. negotiators will meet European and NATO officials in Brussels this week to discuss postwar security guarantees and Ukraine's reconstruction.
